Can #AI Learn from Nature—and Help Us Design a More Resilient Planet?

In 2024, AI consumed over 80 terawatt-hours of electricity—roughly equal to Belgium’s annual consumption. Within just three years, that could soar to 1,000 TWh—enough to power 125 million people, or the entire nation of Japan.

Meanwhile, 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty. That same energy could have powered basic needs—light, refrigeration, connectivity—for every one of them.

So, what kind of intelligence are we investing in?

Nature is not just a resource. It’s the original intelligence. With 3.8 billion years of R&D, nature has evolved systems that are efficient, adaptive, and regenerative.

That’s the promise of planetary design—a new development logic based on integration, not just innovation. As renewable energy systems expand, they are becoming more decentralized, complex, and interdependent—more like ecosystems. AI can serve as the operational brain: forecasting demand, managing complexity, and balancing flows.

At the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  Spring Festival, we reflected on a crucial question:
Will AI learn from nature—or help us forget it faster?

AI should help us see both the forest and the trees—managing trade-offs across water, energy, food, land, and health systems. Here’s how we can shape that future:

⸻

1️⃣ Build local value chains:
Indonesia, home to 21% of the world’s nickel reserves, is transforming mineral wealth into domestic battery and digital manufacturing capacity. UNDP  supports integrated strategies that align clean energy, digital infrastructure, and national development goals.

2️⃣ Invest in smart, distributed energy systems:
In India, AI-powered load forecasting and smart meters are cutting technical losses and outages. In states like Uttar Pradesh and Assam, digital energy management has reduced losses by up to 20% and improved billing for millions.

3️⃣ Develop sovereign, inclusive data ecosystems:
With 2.6 billion people still offline, entire communities remain invisible to AI systems shaping public services. Efforts like Africa’s Masakhane network—building AI in 40+ African languages—are paving the way toward more inclusive digital futures.

4️⃣ Govern AI like we govern ecosystems:
From optimizing illegal logging to deciding who gets access to food or healthcare, AI already impacts lives and global commons. Ethical, inclusive, and transparent AI governance isn’t optional—it’s essential.

⸻

AI should not only optimize—but integrate.
Not just mimic nature—but learn from its logic.

Because intelligence isn’t measured by how much we automate—but by how well we adapt, include, and sustain.

From artificial to planetary intelligence—the future is ours to shape.

#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalDevelopment #JustTransition #DataSovereignty #PlanetaryDesign #AIForGood #NatureBasedSolutions

Women and the $8.75B AI-in-Energy Opportunity: The Time to Act is Now

The global AI-in-energy market is already worth $8.75 billion and is projected to grow by over 30% annually—reaching an estimated $1.3 trillion by 2030. This transformation holds immense potential—not just for accelerating decarbonization, but for unlocking new pathways for women’s leadership, innovation, and economic participation.

And we’re already seeing results.

From Cameroon’s Green Girls Organization, which uses AI to bring off-grid solar and biogas solutions to rural communities, to the UAE’s AI-powered ZERO platform, which helps organizations track emissions and decarbonize, women are already leading the way with real-world examples of how inclusive AI can power inclusive energy transitions.

Yet today, women still represent only one-third of AI professionals and just 20% of the energy workforce—despite comprising 40% of the global labor force. In fast-growing fields like AI, demand surged eightfold in 2024, but only 28% of learners were women. And while 48% of STEM graduates in the Arab region are women, only 20% participate in the labor market. These gaps represent not a constraint—but a vast, untapped opportunity.

There is a clear path forward: 

1️⃣ Inclusive Education & Digital Access: Expanding AI- and energy-focused education—particularly for young women—is vital to building a diverse, future-ready workforce. With the AI-energy market projected to grow rapidly, targeted skilling programmes can address the gender gap in AI pathways and unlock underutilized talent. 

2️⃣ Inclusive Policy & Gender-Disaggregated Data: Gathering gender-specific data and using it to inform policymaking is essential to ensure women aren’t left behind in the AI-energy transition. Data-driven approaches can expose structural disparities, improve pay equity, and inform inclusive skilling and employment strategies—ensuring the transition mobilizes the full spectrum of available talent and leaves no one behind. 

3️⃣ Support for Women-Led Innovation: Fostering women’s participation in AI-energy entrepreneurship is not just about equity—it’s a strategy for accelerating the clean energy transition. As the AI-in-energy market moves toward a $1.3 trillion valuation by 2030, prioritizing investment and support for women-led innovation can drive clean energy adoption while aligning growth with gender equity and sustainable development goals. 

This is more than a moment—it’s a movement. It’s an opportunity to build inclusive AI-energy ecosystems from the ground up, ensuring that policymaking is no longer blind to the full scope of exclusion. The talent is out there; now we need the policies, investments, and support to make this vision a reality.

Africa stands at a pivotal juncture, where the energy transition and digital transformation are not just parallel trends; they are converging revolutions to unlock a new development paradigm.
 
Across Africa, more than 2,000 languages are spoken, with 75 of them having over a million speakers. Yet the AI systems already shaping markets, education, and public services are trained to recognize only a few. This is not just a technical gap; it’s a political one. When technology doesn’t speak your language, it can’t serve your future. That’s why localizing innovation - from data to design - is foundational.
 
Today, at the 2025 Oxford Africa Conference, I had the privilege to reflect on how AI and data technologies can become powerful enablers for a just and inclusive energy transition in Africa. The continent holds over 60% of global solar potential, 30% of the world’s critical mineral reserves, and a youth demographic poised to drive innovation and growth. Yet unlocking this potential requires more than ambition; it demands intentional design, inclusive architecture, and integrated systems:
 
1️⃣ Design for inclusion from the start: Across Africa, MSMEs make up 90% of businesses and 80% of employment. Yet they remain underserved by digital and energy infrastructure. AI systems must be built on local data, adapted to diverse operating contexts and geared toward inclusive growth. Digital tools, when intentionally designed, can extend services and financing to the last mile—turning technology into an equalizer, not a divider.
 
2️⃣ Co-develop digital and energy infrastructure: Energy and AI are not parallel tracks; they are co-dependent systems. We must invest in digital infrastructure powered by renewables and in energy systems optimized by AI. Africa currently accounts for just 1% of global data center capacity, but needs over 700 new centers by 2030. These should be clean-powered, locally managed, and embedded in national development strategies.
 
3️⃣ Move up the value chain in clean technologies: Despite holding 30% of the world’s critical minerals, the continent continues to export raw materials and re-import finished technologies at many times the cost. The future lies in integrated value chains: from mining and processing to battery manufacturing and renewable-powered digital infrastructure. The DRC–Zambia battery corridor offers a model for regionally coordinated value creation.
 
We have the innovation. We have the tools. Now we need to scale them and embed them into the heart of development strategies. The convergence of AI and clean energy isn’t just an opportunity; it’s a catalyst to redefine development outcomes across Africa.
 
The question is no longer whether Africa can lead, but how we ensure that leadership is equitable, sustainable, and strategically designed. 

 
#EnergyForDevelopment  #Digital  #OxfordAfrica2025 Oxford Africa Conference

export-urn-li-share-7332628202659446784.caption:
In 2024, a power outage in the Maldives caused a 50-hour disruption of water. Not because of water scarcity, but because the electric pumps failed. Meanwhile, Roman aqueducts built +2,000 years ago were still functioning with no grid; no software; and no emissions.
 
So, we ought to ask ourselves: are today’s systems more advanced - or just more fragile?
 
Last week, at the TIDE Senior Advisors Retreat, I had the privilege to reflect on what really counts as innovation - and what happens when we optimize systems that leave people behind? Because the real question isn’t whether to innovate or optimize. It’s whether we are building energy systems that are resilient, inclusive, and future-ready. Here’s what we explored:
 
1️⃣ Innovation and optimization are interdependent. Solar PV costs fell 90% between 2008 and 2022. But innovation alone doesn’t decarbonize cities. Optimization, through smart meters, AI forecasting, and grid balancing, is what enables real-time impact.
 
2️⃣ Technology must deliver equity, not just efficiency. The top 10% of global energy users consume 20x more than the bottom 10%. Yet solutions are emerging: AI-powered tariffs from M-KOPA in Kenya, energy-efficient appliances in South Africa, mobile-enabled solar in Bangladesh.
 
3️⃣ Innovation must be guided by governance. AI can predict renewable variability with 90% accuracy. But without inclusive policy and regulation, it can also deprioritize vulnerable communities.
 
Optimization and innovation must go hand in hand with development. This is not just about technology. It is about justice and systems that serve everyone.
 So, the real question is: What are we optimizing for? Megawatts, or human wellbeing?
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalDevelopment #justtransition

Can Africa lead two revolutions at once - digital and energy?

This bold question was at the heart of an inspiring panel at the Oxford Africa Conference 2025, moderated by Tin El Kadi, with insights from Mr. Riad Meddeb , Dr. Amir Lebdioui , and Dr. Romelle Horton.

Did you know that across Africa, more than 2,000 languages are spoken, with 75 of them having over a million speakers? Yet the AI systems being deployed today, already shaping markets, education, and public services, are trained to recognize only a few. As Riad Meddeb reminded us that the convergence of AI and clean energy isn’t just an opportunity; it’s a catalyst to redefine development outcomes across Africa. But to truly unlock this potential, we must invest in inclusive digital design, interconnected digital–energy infrastructure, and strategic value creation across supply chains.

And as Dr. Amir Lebdioui noted there are more African engineers in the U.S. than in all of Africa. That striking reality reveals that this is not about a lack of capabilities; it’s about how we nurture ecosystems and make use of existing skills.

We have the innovation. We have the talent. Now is the time to scale locally, and build a future where Africa doesn’t just join these revolutions but leads them.

🎥 I highly recommend watching the full recording of this excellent discussion here: https://lnkd.in/dUgVHh8w #OxfordAfricaConference #EnergyforDevelopment

Green hydrogen is booming. But is it truly driving a green revolution—or are we creating a global climate illusion?

Over 50 countries now have national hydrogen strategies, and by 2050, the global hydrogen trade could be worth $280 billion. Yet progress is uneven: 83% of current investments are concentrated in Europe and China, and fewer than 7% of announced projects have reached operation.

As momentum builds, it is crucial that local governments—especially in the Global South—have the tools, evidence, and agency to shape hydrogen pathways that reflect their development priorities. That’s why, together with Amir Lebdioui  and Pavel Bilek  I recently joined a conversation with Martin Lambert  Head of Hydrogen Research at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, to explore the findings of a new collaborative approach between UNDP  and TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  on green hydrogen.

As part of this work, we are developing practical guidelines to support local governments in navigating the development impacts of their hydrogen strategies—ensuring that national ambition translates into inclusive, context-specific outcomes on the ground. Hydrogen can be a powerful driver of inclusive and sustainable development if shaped deliberately and guided by the right evidence. Here’s how:

1️⃣ A Catalyst for Inclusive Growth
Green hydrogen can unlock significant economic opportunities. In South Africa, projections suggest a 3.6% increase in GDP and 370,000 new jobs by 2050. But realizing these benefits depends on building local value chains, investing in skills development, and designing policies that prioritize domestic gains—not just global supply.

2️⃣ A Climate Solution with Resource Realities
Hydrogen is key to decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. Yet it is resource-intensive: producing 1 kg of green hydrogen requires about 9 liters of purified water. Supporting countries to align hydrogen investments with local resource constraints—especially in water-stressed regions—is critical to long-term sustainability.

3️⃣ A Risk of Widening Inequality
Today, 83% of global electrolysis investments are concentrated in Europe and China. Without deliberate action, the hydrogen economy risks reinforcing global divides. But there’s also an opportunity: with the right strategies, countries can leapfrog legacy systems. In some contexts, direct electrification or alternative industrial pathways may be more viable.

The energy transition isn’t just about technology—it’s about people, priorities, and power. By asking the right questions and equipping local actors with the right tools, we can shape a hydrogen future that is just, inclusive, and grounded in real-world development goals.

#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustTransition #ClimateAction #FutureOfEnergy

The electric vehicle (EV) revolution is well underway, signaling a transformative shift in global transportation and energy systems. Just last year, EVs accounted for over 20% of all car sales globally, and nearly 1 in 2 new cars sold in China was electric.
 
However, as we move towards 2030, the growing demand for EVs also signals an imminent surge in battery demand, set to grow by 6–10X, posing a potential twin-challenge & opportunity for critical mineral use and extraction. Yet in this context, Solid-State Batteries (SSB) emerge as an enabling technology, offering up to five times the energy density of conventional lithium-ion batteries. Solid-state batteries offer significant advantages that align with global sustainable development priorities:
 
1️⃣Enhanced Performance and Safety:
SSBs provide higher energy density; faster charging times; and improved thermal stability, reducing risks associated with lithium-ion batteries. Their robustness across temperature ranges and extended lifespans also make them ideal for grid-scale energy storage, facilitating greater integration of renewable energy sources and enhancing grid resilience.
 
2️⃣Cross-sectoral Innovation:
The compact size and enhanced performance of SSBs present opportunities beyond EV applications including: electric aviation, shipping and even consumer electronics, enabling longer operational life and increased safety.
 
3️⃣Environmental Sustainability:
By minimizing reliance on flammable liquid electrolytes and reducing the demand for scarce minerals, SSBs contribute to lowering the environmental footprint of battery production and disposal, supporting circular economy principles.
 
The global push for solid-state battery innovation reflects a broader truth: clean energy transitions are no longer national ambitions, they are shared imperatives. Strategic investments from India, research partnerships between Brazil & Singapore, and cross-sector collaboration signal a growing recognition that technology must serve inclusive, sustainable development.
 
Solid-state batteries hold the promise not just of better performance, but of decarbonizing mobility, strengthening energy resilience, and accelerating progress toward SDG7. To find out more about this technology in greater detail, I invite you to read this previous collaborative blog on Deep Tech Series: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eXViZjKg

Decentralized Renewable Energy is more than a technology. It's a pathway to equity, resilience and economic transformation.

As we confront the urgency of climate action and global inequality, Decentralized Renewable Energy (DRE) emerges as one of the most transformative tools for sustainable development. At the intersection of technology, equity, and climate resilience, DRE offers an opportunity to radically rethink how energy is produced, distributed, and owned - especially in the Global South

Today, 685 million people still live without electricity and over 1.18 billion endure energy poverty; struggling to power irrigation for food security, digital tools for learning and/or essential equipment in health facilities. But as we accelerate toward universal energy access, how we achieve this goal is just as important as how fast we achieve it. 

The Global South has the opportunity to leapfrog fossil fuels and centralized grid models to design systems that prioritize justice, resilience, and local empowerment:

🔹 Empowering communities as energy "prosumers":
DRE allows households and communities to generate, use, and even sell electricity; breaking away from dependency on centralized grids and enabling more equitable energy participation. This shift not only democratizes energy production but also reduces energy access disparities.

🌊 As we mark #WorldOceansDay and the launch of the 2025 UN Ocean Conference in Nice, we have a pivotal opportunity: to align ocean health with the global energy transition.

The ocean is a foundation of life on Earth. It covers 75% of the planet; generates 50% of our oxygen; absorbs 30% of CO2 emissions; and supports +150 million jobs worldwide. It provides food, energy and critical resources to billions - yet remains under threat from rising temperatures, acidification, pollution, overexploitation and biodiversity loss.

If the ocean economy were a country, it would be the fifth largest economy in the world. That level of economic and environmental significance calls for bold, integrated responses. Here’s where development action can accelerate meaningful impact:

1️⃣ Decarbonize Maritime Transport as a Catalyst for Clean Energy Systems:
Maritime transport emits over 1GtCO2 annually (around 2.9% of global emissions) and is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize due to fossil fuel reliance and long asset lifecycles. To align with the Paris Agreement, zero-emission fuels need to make up 5% of international and 15% of domestic shipping by 2030. Transitioning to clean fuels can transform shipping from a major emitter into a catalyst for clean energy investment, innovation, and industrial demand, contributing directly to system-wide decarbonization and reducing global GHG emissions by 3-5% by 2030. 

2️⃣ Transform Ports into Clean Energy Hubs for a Just Transition:
Strategic clean fuel corridors can anchor renewable deployment, storage and grid upgrades at ports - especially in Small Island Developing States, where ocean-based exports account for 16% of GDP. Port electrification enhances climate resilience, connects maritime and energy planning, and ensures vulnerable economies benefit from the energy transition.

3️⃣ Integrate Maritime Decarbonization into Global Energy Finance:
Despite their potential, maritime and ocean-based clean energy solutions remain underfunded. In 2022, global clean energy investments reached  $2.1 trillion; yet < 1% was directed towards maritime energy developments. Offshore wind alone could grow from $39.6B in 2024 to $146B by 2031, powering up to 1.5B homes annually by 2050 and driving inclusive growth across coastal regions - especially in the Global South. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can unlock scalable pathways for maritime decarbonization and clean energy innovation at sea.

Decarbonization is critical, not only for SDG 13  and SDG 14, but for resilient, inclusive development. 

As we look toward this 2025 UN Ocean Conference, we must raise ambition; align public and private finance; and unlock innovation across the blue economy. A healthy ocean is not only vital for biodiversity. It is fundamental to a just energy transition

The ocean cannot wait - and neither can we.

 #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #MaritimeDecarbonization #SDG14

Offshore wind energy is more than a climate solution; it’s a strategic lever for national development, maritime decarbonization and long-term energy security. By 2030, global offshore wind capacity is projected to reach 212 GW, nearly quadrupling the 73 GW recorded in 2023. Annual additions are anticipated to grow from 9.5 GW in 2023 to over 45 GW by 2030, with China driving half the growth and Europe, the U.S., Japan and Korea emerging as key markets.

Yet, despite this momentum, offshore wind faces high capital costs; long lead times; and permitting barriers - especially in the Global South. These challenges have slowed momentum and shifted investor interest toward faster-moving solar PV projects.
 
Globally, if current commitments are realized, offshore wind could power +1.5 billion homes annually by 2050. But to make this a truly global solution - especially for emerging and climate-vulnerable economies - urgent action is needed across three key areas:

1️⃣ Integrate Offshore Wind into National Energy and Development Plans: Embedding offshore wind in long-term national energy strategies helps align permitting, grid infrastructure, and port development - making projects more investable. In 2023 alone, $33.75 billion was invested in offshore wind globally. With supportive policies, countries can attract a greater share of this capital while linking wind energy to jobs, exports, and green industrialization.


2️⃣ Scale Floating Wind to Unlock Untapped Resources: Traditional offshore wind turbines are fixed to the seabed in shallow waters, excluding many countries with deep coastal zones. Floating wind technology could allow for turbines to be installed further from shore, opening access to major wind resources in regions like Southeast Asia, West Africa and SIDS. As floating technology becomes more affordable, early investment and pilot projects can help bring these regions into the global offshore wind market. 


3️⃣ Use Public-Private Finance to De-risk and Attract Investment: At around $3,461/kW, offshore wind remains nearly three times as expensive as onshore alternatives. Such high upfront costs make it harder for new markets to compete. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can improve project economics and unlock long-term returns. With the right financial tools, offshore wind can scale  in regions where clean energy access is most needed.

Offshore wind isn’t just about clean electricity: it’s about building resilient economies, powering green industries, and creating a just transition.

The Global South holds vast offshore wind potential. With the right policies and partnerships, we can turn this into a catalyst for clean industrialization, energy security, and inclusive growth.

#EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #OffshoreWind #MaritimeEnergy

What if the ocean isn’t just a climate risk, but a climate solution - and Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are already leading the way? SIDS may contribute <1% of global emissions, but their vast marine territories, abundant renewable resources and closely connected communities uniquely position them to pioneer solutions that are not only green, but also blue - integrating clean energy with ocean-based economies. From solar-chilled cold storage for fisheries in the Maldives to digital platforms in the Caribbean SIDS that use satellite data to guide sustainable marine planning, SIDS are showing that size is no barrier to impact.
 
@UNDP’s “Blue Economy for Green Islands” approach connects renewable energy with ocean-based industries to drive low-carbon, inclusive growth. By leveraging wind, solar, tidal, and ocean thermal energy, SIDS can diversify economies and decarbonize maritime sectors. Within this integrated framework, three transformative solutions stand out:
 
 
1️⃣ Whole-Island Renewable Ecosystems: Linking clean energy with ocean sectors like aquaculture, desalination, eco-tourism, and transport can cut emissions and boost livelihoods. Ocean industries already generate 16% of SIDS’ GDP. In Vanuatu and Cabo Verde, solar-powered fisheries and irrigation systems are strengthening food security, reduce emissions and expand local jobs. These systems also benefit women, who make up 52% of SIDS’ agricultural workforce, advancing gender equity and delivering gender-responsive benefits
 
 
2️⃣ Microgrids for Disaster Resilience: Decentralized systems like hybrid mini-grids are vital in SIDS, where disasters cause $1.6B in yearly losses. Vanuatu’s solar-hydro mini-grid powers schools, clinics, and markets for 50,000+ people. Such systems help close the SDG 7 access gap, which still affects 9% of SIDS’ populations, especially in rural areas.
 
 
3️⃣ Invest in #Ocean-Based Renewables: Offshore wind, tidal, and ocean thermal energy make up <2% of installed capacity in SIDS, despite vast potential. Scaling them can power ports, ferries, and aquaculture - creating low-carbon energy loops. Innovative finance tools like blue bonds, debt-for-energy swaps, and blended finance can de-risk investments and scale projects
 
The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS calls for placing sustainable energy at the heart of development, with many SIDS already leading the way towards 100% renewable energy in their power mix by 2030.

In 2024, the world added over 585 GW of renewables, and clean energy jobs surpassed 16 million. Solar is now the least expensive electricity source in history and global energy investments are expected to reach $3.3 trillion by 2025. This is more than a technology shift; it's a global economic transformation.
 
But one critical question remains: Are we making the energy transition work for everyone, everywhere?
 
In Mongolia, coal still dominates the energy system. In Ulaanbaatar, 1.6M people rely on raw coal for heat - driving pollution 27x over WHO limits, causing 7,000+ premature deaths and costing 10% of GDP.  Despite these challenges, Mongolia has committed to change - targeting 30% renewable energy by 2030.
 
That’s why, at the recent Multistakeholder Workshop on Advancing a Just Energy Transition in Mongolia - co-hosted by Mongolia’s Ministry of Energy and UNDP - I shared four ways on how to reposition these challenges as opportunities for a just and inclusive transition:
 
1️⃣ Finance That Unlocks Scale:
By 2023, Mongolia attracted $533M across 12 utility-scale renewables. However renewables in Mongolia face high capital costs and limited de-risking. Green bonds, sovereign guarantees, and blended finance (like Paraguay’s $150M e-bus model from $20M in seed funding) can mobilize clean energy investment at scale.
 
2️⃣ Urban Energy That Protects Lives:
Coal-based systems drive both pollution and inequality. Ulaanbaatar’s air crisis is a public health emergency. A just transition must deliver clean heating, efficient housing, and e-mobility. UNDP pilots show solar + battery + insulation can cut emissions and protect over half the country’s population.
 
3️⃣ Digital Tools for Smart Equity:
Energy demand grew 4.7% per capita in one year. Mongolia’s vast geography needs digital planning. AI and geospatial tools - like smart meters in Chingeltei that track carbon savings -can guide clean energy to off-grid and low-income areas, just as UNDP is doing in Moldova.
 
4️⃣ Fossil Fuel Subsidy Reforms:
In Mongolia, fossil fuel subsidies reached $9B in 2023; a 120% increase since 2018. Yet by fully phasing them out, we could free up 3.6% of global GDP for reinvestment. With UNDP’s support, countries like Mongolia are designing reforms that reinvest from e-mobility to human capital and health systems.  
 
A just transition is about people, not just power. It’s about shaping a future where energy delivers jobs, health, resilience and dignity. Across Mongolia and Asia-Pacific, @UNDP is helping make that future a reality, ensuring no one is left behind.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #Mongolia #GreenFinance #DigitalForDevelopment

At a marine testing site in Scotland, 20 Oyster wave energy converters have the potential to power 12,000 homes. Now imagine the transformative potential if Small Island Developing States (SIDS) - surrounded by ocean, rich in wave and tidal resources - could harness these innovations at scale?
 
Ocean-based energy technologies are fast becoming a practical solution to some of the world’s most pressing challenges: energy security, climate resilience and economic development. For SIDS, which face some of the highest energy costs globally, and are among the most vulnerable to climate change, these technologies offer a triple win; sustainable power, economic opportunity, and strengthened resilience.

🔹 Tonga is developing a 10-MW wave power park in Tongatapu - set to meet 50% of its energy needs and cut emissions by 20%.
 
🔹 Barbados is exploring Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), integrating it into a broader blue economy strategy supported by @UNDP and SIDS DOCK.
 
🔹 Seychelles is piloting the first floating solar PV project on lagoon waters, laying the groundwork for hybrid marine energy solutions through its marine spatial planning framework.
 
These are not isolated experiments. They are scalable, replicable and exemplify what’s possible when innovation meets local ambition and global support.
 
To see other success stores and find out how else SIDS are redefining development pathways, I  invite you to read this UNDP Policy Paper: 👉 go.undp.org/34Q

That’s why, at the recent Multistakeholder Workshop on Advancing a Just Energy Transition in Mongolia - co-hosted by Mongolia’s Ministry of Energy and UNDP - I shared four ways on how to reposition these challenges as opportunities for a just and inclusive transition:
 
1️⃣ Finance That Unlocks Scale:
By 2023, Mongolia attracted $533M across 12 utility-scale renewables. However renewables in Mongolia face high capital costs and limited de-risking. Green bonds, sovereign guarantees, and blended finance (like Paraguay’s $150M e-bus model from $20M in seed funding) can mobilize clean energy investment at scale.
 
2️⃣ Urban Energy That Protects Lives:
Coal-based systems drive both pollution and inequality. Ulaanbaatar’s air crisis is a public health emergency. A just transition must deliver clean heating, efficient housing, and e-mobility. UNDP pilots show solar + battery + insulation can cut emissions and protect over half the country’s population.
 
3️⃣ Digital Tools for Smart Equity:
Energy demand grew 4.7% per capita in one year. Mongolia’s vast geography needs digital planning. AI and geospatial tools - like smart meters in Chingeltei that track carbon savings -can guide clean energy to off-grid and low-income areas, just as UNDP is doing in Moldova.
 
4️⃣ Fossil Fuel Subsidy Reforms:
In Mongolia, fossil fuel subsidies reached $9B in 2023; a 120% increase since 2018. Yet by fully phasing them out, we could free up 3.6% of global GDP for reinvestment. With UNDP’s support, countries like Mongolia are designing reforms that reinvest from e-mobility to human capital and health systems.  
 
A just transition is about people, not just power. It’s about shaping a future where energy delivers jobs, health, resilience and dignity. Across Mongolia and Asia-Pacific, @UNDP is helping make that future a reality, ensuring no one is left behind. #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #Mongolia #GreenFinance #DigitalForDevelopment

🌊 As we mark #WorldOceansDay and the launch of the 2025 UN Ocean Conference in Nice, we have a pivotal opportunity: to align ocean health with the global energy transition.

The ocean is a foundation of life on Earth. It covers 75% of the planet; generates 50% of our oxygen; absorbs 30% of CO2 emissions; and supports +150 million jobs worldwide. It provides food, energy and critical resources to billions - yet remains under threat from rising temperatures, acidification, pollution, overexploitation and biodiversity loss.

If the ocean economy were a country, it would be the fifth largest economy in the world. That level of economic and environmental significance calls for bold, integrated responses. Here’s where development action can accelerate meaningful impact:

1️⃣ Decarbonize Maritime Transport as a Catalyst for Clean Energy Systems:
Maritime transport emits over 1GtCO2 annually (around 2.9% of global emissions) and is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize due to fossil fuel reliance and long asset lifecycles. To align with the Paris Agreement, zero-emission fuels need to make up 5% of international and 15% of domestic shipping by 2030. Transitioning to clean fuels can transform shipping from a major emitter into a catalyst for clean energy investment, innovation, and industrial demand, contributing directly to system-wide decarbonization and reducing global GHG emissions by 3-5% by 2030. 

2️⃣ Transform Ports into Clean Energy Hubs for a Just Transition:
Strategic clean fuel corridors can anchor renewable deployment, storage and grid upgrades at ports - especially in Small Island Developing States, where ocean-based exports account for 16% of GDP. Port electrification enhances climate resilience, connects maritime and energy planning, and ensures vulnerable economies benefit from the energy transition.

3️⃣ Integrate Maritime Decarbonization into Global Energy Finance:
Despite their potential, maritime and ocean-based clean energy solutions remain underfunded. In 2022, global clean energy investments reached  $2.1 trillion; yet < 1% was directed towards maritime energy developments. Offshore wind alone could grow from $39.6B in 2024 to $146B by 2031, powering up to 1.5B homes annually by 2050 and driving inclusive growth across coastal regions - especially in the Global South. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can unlock scalable pathways for maritime decarbonization and clean energy innovation at sea.

Decarbonization is critical, not only for SDG 13  and SDG 14, but for resilient, inclusive development. 

As we look toward this 2025 UN Ocean Conference, we must raise ambition; align public and private finance; and unlock innovation across the blue economy. A healthy ocean is not only vital for biodiversity. It is fundamental to a just energy transition

The ocean cannot wait - and neither can we. #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #MaritimeDecarbonization #SDG14

Offshore wind energy is more than a climate solution; it’s a strategic lever for national development, maritime decarbonization and long-term energy security. By 2030, global offshore wind capacity is projected to reach 212 GW, nearly quadrupling the 73 GW recorded in 2023. Annual additions are anticipated to grow from 9.5 GW in 2023 to over 45 GW by 2030, with China driving half the growth and Europe, the U.S., Japan and Korea emerging as key markets.

Yet, despite this momentum, offshore wind faces high capital costs; long lead times; and permitting barriers - especially in the Global South. These challenges have slowed momentum and shifted investor interest toward faster-moving solar PV projects.
 
Globally, if current commitments are realized, offshore wind could power +1.5 billion homes annually by 2050. But to make this a truly global solution - especially for emerging and climate-vulnerable economies - urgent action is needed across three key areas:

1️⃣ Integrate Offshore Wind into National Energy and Development Plans: Embedding offshore wind in long-term national energy strategies helps align permitting, grid infrastructure, and port development - making projects more investable. In 2023 alone, $33.75 billion was invested in offshore wind globally. With supportive policies, countries can attract a greater share of this capital while linking wind energy to jobs, exports, and green industrialization.


2️⃣ Scale Floating Wind to Unlock Untapped Resources: Traditional offshore wind turbines are fixed to the seabed in shallow waters, excluding many countries with deep coastal zones. Floating wind technology could allow for turbines to be installed further from shore, opening access to major wind resources in regions like Southeast Asia, West Africa and SIDS. As floating technology becomes more affordable, early investment and pilot projects can help bring these regions into the global offshore wind market. 


3️⃣ Use Public-Private Finance to De-risk and Attract Investment: At around $3,461/kW, offshore wind remains nearly three times as expensive as onshore alternatives. Such high upfront costs make it harder for new markets to compete. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can improve project economics and unlock long-term returns. With the right financial tools, offshore wind can scale  in regions where clean energy access is most needed.

Offshore wind isn’t just about clean electricity: it’s about building resilient economies, powering green industries, and creating a just transition.

The Global South holds vast offshore wind potential. With the right policies and partnerships, we can turn this into a catalyst for clean industrialization, energy security, and inclusive growth. #EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #OffshoreWind #MaritimeEnergy

The global shift to renewables is essential- but it must also be equitable. Cobalt and lithium are critical to clean technologies, yet their extraction often harms people and ecosystems. By 2050, the world will need 3x more cobalt and up to 40x lithium (compared to 2020 levels) driven by the needs of batteries, solar, wind, data centres and EVs .

In the DRC, which supplies over 70% of global cobalt, mining has polluted rivers, harmed crops and triggered human rights abuses -  including child labor. In Chile’s Atacama Desert, lithium operations have cut freshwater availability by 65%, threatening biodiversity and Indigenous livelihoods. 

This raises a critical question: how can we transition to a low-carbon future without deepening the nature and inequality crises? To ensure the clean energy transition is also a just transition, we must adopt integrated system-level solutions:

🔁 Closed-loop material systems can help reduce new extraction. Currently, only 1% of lithium and < 5% of cobalt is recycled from end-of-life batteries. Circular economy models - from battery reuse to advanced recycling - are essential to reduce demand for virgin mining.

🌍 Local value additions must be prioritized. Despite holding over half of global cobalt and manganese reserves,  Africa captures <5% of the global battery value chain. With battery demand set to triple by 2030, countries with an abundance of critical minerals should not be confined to raw extraction alone. By investing in local refining, battery production and and knowledge transfer, these countries can generate jobs, retain more economic value and reduce export dependency.

⚡ Smarter, greener grids are also important. Renewable energy sources are inherently variable. Next-generation energy efficient grids, such as AI-powered smart grids, can help balance supply and demand more effectively, reducing energy waste and integrating diverse power sources at scale.

The energy transition offers a once-in-a-generation opportunity to tackle climate change but only if it’s done in a way that is fair, inclusive and sustainable. To find out how mining can contribute to a just transition for both people and the planet, I invite you to read the Just Transition edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/ey8b-Dds

Energy access is not just a technology challenge; it’s a matter of equity, regional cooperation, and economic opportunity.

Globally, 685 million people still lack access to electricity—80% of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. At the current pace, 660 million people could remain unelectrified by 2030, the vast majority in Africa. This is not merely a technical gap; it’s a development crisis that impacts health, education, livelihoods, and resilience.

But this is also a moment of unprecedented opportunity.

Africa holds extraordinary clean energy potential. Countries like Ethiopia and the DRC possess over 80 GW of hydropower potential, while the Sahel region enjoys some of the highest solar irradiance on Earth. Yet, between 2002 and 2020, Africa received less than 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewable energy. Cross-border electricity trade remains limited, with just 10 GW of transmission capacity—compared to 127 GW in Europe.

This raises a critical question: how can we close the energy access gap without reinforcing inequality and fragmentation?
The answer lies in a just, integrated energy transition—where regional power trade becomes a catalyst for shared prosperity. And the solutions are within reach:

1️⃣ Invest in Cross-Border Infrastructure:
Regional power trading can reduce electricity supply costs by up to 30%, accelerating access in underserved areas. In the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), countries like Namibia and Botswana are already importing affordable hydropower from Zambia and Mozambique, enhancing both affordability and reliability.

2️⃣ Mobilize Inclusive Finance & Guarantees:
Bridging Africa’s $25 billion annual clean energy investment gap requires more than capital. Concessional finance, de-risking mechanisms, and technical assistance are critical to enabling LDCs to participate in regional markets and scale up electrification.

3️⃣ Leverage Regional Comparative Advantage:
Countries such as Ethiopia and the DRC generate more clean power than they consume, and the Sahel’s solar potential exceeds 2,200 kWh/m²/year. Regional trade allows these countries to monetize surplus energy, promote industrialization, and generate revenues that can support local development.

This is a defining moment. The energy access challenge is no longer just about generation—it’s about connection, cooperation, and coordination. With the right policies and targeted investments, Africa can shift from energy poverty to regional power prosperity, while advancing climate action and inclusive growth.

To learn how energy access and trade can transform economies and lives, I invite you to explore the latest insights here:  👉 https://lnkd.in/epaxVxyJ

🌱 Today’s #energy panel at the #Sustainable Finance Policy Dialogue in Samoa was a blast! 🔋⚡

Energy access is not just a technology challenge; it’s a matter of equity, regional cooperation, and economic opportunity.

Globally, 685 million people still lack access to electricity—80% of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. At the current pace, 660 million people could remain unelectrified by 2030, the vast majority in Africa. This is not merely a technical gap; it’s a development crisis that impacts health, education, livelihoods, and resilience.

But this is also a moment of unprecedented opportunity.

Africa holds extraordinary clean energy potential. Countries like Ethiopia and the DRC possess over 80 GW of hydropower potential, while the Sahel region enjoys some of the highest solar irradiance on Earth. Yet, between 2002 and 2020, Africa received less than 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewable energy. Cross-border electricity trade remains limited, with just 10 GW of transmission capacity—compared to 127 GW in Europe.

This raises a critical question: how can we close the energy access gap without reinforcing inequality and fragmentation?
The answer lies in a just, integrated energy transition—where regional power trade becomes a catalyst for shared prosperity. And the solutions are within reach:

1️⃣ Invest in Cross-Border Infrastructure:
Regional power trading can reduce electricity supply costs by up to 30%, accelerating access in underserved areas. In the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), countries like Namibia and Botswana are already importing affordable hydropower from Zambia and Mozambique, enhancing both affordability and reliability.

2️⃣ Mobilize Inclusive Finance & Guarantees:
Bridging Africa’s $25 billion annual clean energy investment gap requires more than capital. Concessional finance, de-risking mechanisms, and technical assistance are critical to enabling LDCs to participate in regional markets and scale up electrification.

3️⃣ Leverage Regional Comparative Advantage:
Countries such as Ethiopia and the DRC generate more clean power than they consume, and the Sahel’s solar potential exceeds 2,200 kWh/m²/year. Regional trade allows these countries to monetize surplus energy, promote industrialization, and generate revenues that can support local development.

This is a defining moment. The energy access challenge is no longer just about generation—it’s about connection, cooperation, and coordination. With the right policies and targeted investments, Africa can shift from energy poverty to regional power prosperity, while advancing climate action and inclusive growth.

Planning energy transitions without sufficient data is like trying to navigate in the dark.
 
Despite decades of progress, over 685 million people still lack access to electricity. Traditional data sources - household surveys, national censuses, static infrastructure maps - are too slow, too sparse, or too disconnected from on-the-ground realities to be able to accurately make investments and optimize projects.
 
To address this, UNDP  partnered with IBM  to co-develop two data-driven tools now featured in the International Energy Agency (IEA)  ’s new Energy & AI Observatory👉🏾 https://lnkd.in/e3yJs_Q4. 
These models represent a digital shift, as AI and open data enable a just energy transition through grounding data-driven actions in approaches that leave no one behind:
 
  1. Clean Energy Equity Index Developed with IBM and Stony Brook University, this tool generates an equity score at the subnational level across 53 African countries, combining data on education, income, emissions, and infrastructure. The index helps identify regions where clean energy investment will have the most equitable and transformative impact.
 
  2. Electricity Access Forecasting Model Built with IBM watsonx and trained on satellite imagery, infrastructure data, population growth, and land use dynamics, this model delivers hyper-granular (1 km²) forecasts to 2030 across 102 Global South countries. It enables governments to anticipate demand and prioritize underserved areas long before gaps become crises.
 
Both tools are now accessible through GeoHub, UNDP’s open data platform for geospatial intelligence. https://lnkd.in/erh3Qmny. Moving forward, the challenge will be how we can embed these tools into institutional decision-making, financing frameworks, and policy design.

🌿 Like Thailand’s Ratchaphruek tree, which blooms in synchrony under intense heat, Thailand’s energy transition is unfolding with resilience and purpose. Nature teaches us that thriving under pressure is possible — and Thailand is showing how to turn that lesson into inclusive, future-ready systems.

Grateful to join the Government of Thailand and national stakeholders in advancing a Just Energy Transition rooted in opportunity, equity, and long-term development. This is not just about megawatts — it’s about people, jobs, and systems that deliver for all.

🚀 Thailand is turning ambition into action across four key areas:

🔹 Aligning policies and scaling regional cooperation
To meet its 30% renewable electricity target by 2037, Thailand must deploy 32 GW of new capacity and mobilize $22B in investment. It is advancing integration across energy, climate, and industrial planning — while activating the ASEAN Power Grid and unlocking $1.3B via the ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility.

🔹 Deploying decentralized, people-first systems
With 20 GW rooftop solar potential and hydro-solar-battery pilots like Ubol Ratana, Thailand is cutting emissions and lowering rural electricity costs — currently up to 17% higher than in Bangkok — while boosting grid resilience.

🔹 Championing in cooling efficiency and digital growth
$2.7B in data center investments and surging cooling demand are driving clean innovation. From energy-efficient hospitals to green data hubs, Thailand is turning high energy use into climate-smart infrastructure.

🔹 Empowering SMEs and building green jobs
With 3.1M SMEs and over 230,000 EVs in 2024, Thailand is linking energy transition to entrepreneurship, regional value chains, and inclusive job creation. A just transition could generate over 172,000 renewable energy jobs by 2050, strengthening local economies.

At @UNDP, we are proud to support this journey — through policy, finance, and local capacity. Thailand is not just transitioning. It’s leading.

Let’s ensure Thailand’s energy future is not just greener, but fairer. Not just resilient, but just. ⚡🌏

Cleaner Air, Healthier Lives, Stronger Economies: Why We Need A Clean Energy Transition.
 
Every day, over 90% of the world’s population breathes unhealthy air, with air quality in many countries frequently exceeding dangerous thresholds (AQI >200); largely due to fossil fuel combustion. But the solutions are here, and the benefits are transformational.
 
Every breath of clean air is a right - not a privilege. Clean energy is a catalyst for climate action, human development and economic opportunity. Here’s how:
 
⚡️ Investing in renewables can bring substantial returns: Solar PV alone is now avoiding 1.4 Gt of CO₂ annually - proof that scaling renewables delivers fast impact. With continued investment in wind, e-mobility and heat pumps, we can slash both emissions and air pollution.
 
⚡️ Improved energy access means better health and cleaner skies: Achieving #SDG7 by 2030 could cut air pollution exposure by 75%, prevent 3.6 million premature deaths each year and unlock new jobs and opportunities; especially for the Global South.
 
⚡️ Resilient healthcare can be powered by clean energy: Clean power for hospitals will mean healthier people and fewer emissions. In regions like Sub-Saharan Africa, where 15% of health facilities lack electricity, clean energy can save lives and strengthen systems.
 
⚡️ Targeting methane and black carbon can improve air quality quickly: Cleaner cookstoves, smart methane regulation and support for transitions in fossil sectors can improve air quality quickly. In the continent of Africa alone, shifting to clean cooking fuels could save $66B/year and prevent 463,000 deaths annually - for just $8B a year.
 
⚡️ Digitalization and AI can be fueled by renewables: As data center electricity use is expected to double in the next year, powering them with renewables creates a new frontier: climate-smart digital infrastructure. A clean energy transition keeps us future-ready,  both economically and technologically.
 
At UNDP  we are proud to work alongside governments and communities to turn energy transitions into inclusive, clean-air development stories; from methane action in Turkmenistan to healthcare electrification in Africa.
 
The solutions are proven. The technologies are ready. The benefits  for health, jobs & the planet are substantial. Let’s build a world where clean energy means clean air for everyone, everywhere.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanEnergy #AirQuality #HealthAndEnergy

The latest Tracking SDG7 Progress Report reminds us that the global energy transition is not only a climate imperative but a development necessity.
 
Despite some progress, the world currently remains off track to meet #SDG7. As of 2023, 666 million people still lack access to electricity, and 2.1 billion rely on polluting fuels for cooking. These numbers are not just statistics: they represent lost opportunities for health, education, productivity and dignity. They provide us with both a reality check and a roadmap forward - which is where our focus must be:
 
🔋 Decentralized renewable energy (DRE) is already delivering results:
Between 2020 and 2022, DRE solutions accounted for +50% of new electricity connections in Sub-Saharan Africa. These technologies are affordable, resilient and ready to scale. With the right policy frameworks and investment flows, they can close the access gap in rural and underserved communities fast.
 
💰 Clean energy finance is growing - but it must be better targeted:
Global public finance for clean energy reached $21.6 billion in 2023, even amid economic and geopolitical instability. While incredibly promising, <10% reached EMDEs (excluding China). We need more concessional capital, blended finance models and de-risking tools to drive equitable investment where it’s needed most.
 
🍳 Clean cooking is rising on the agenda - and rightly so:
With only 7% of rural populations in Sub-Saharan Africa accessing clean fuels, now is the time to prioritize solutions that reduce health risks, empower women and support climate goals. Targeted investments in innovation and affordability can shift millions toward safer cooking practices.
 
At @UNDP, we see energy as a catalyst. Our integrated approach to sustainable energy is about more than about powering homes; it’s about unlocking futures. It’s about delivering health systems, schools, jobs, clean air, gender equality and climate resilience.
 
When we invest in energy for development, we multiply impact across the SDGs. What’s missing isn’t technology or resources: it’s urgency  and the willingness to act.  If we rise to the challenge and prioritize a just and inclusive energy transition, we can shape a future for people and planet where no one is left behind.

The electric vehicle (EV) revolution is well underway, signaling a transformative shift in global transportation and energy systems. Just last year, EVs accounted for over 20% of all car sales globally, and nearly 1 in 2 new cars sold in China was electric.
 
However, as we move towards 2030, the growing demand for EVs also signals an imminent surge in battery demand, set to grow by 6–10X, posing a potential twin-challenge & opportunity for critical mineral use and extraction. Yet in this context, Solid-State Batteries (SSB) emerge as an enabling technology, offering up to five times the energy density of conventional lithium-ion batteries. Solid-state batteries offer significant advantages that align with global sustainable development priorities:
 
1️⃣Enhanced Performance and Safety:
SSBs provide higher energy density; faster charging times; and improved thermal stability, reducing risks associated with lithium-ion batteries. Their robustness across temperature ranges and extended lifespans also make them ideal for grid-scale energy storage, facilitating greater integration of renewable energy sources and enhancing grid resilience.
 
2️⃣Cross-sectoral Innovation:
The compact size and enhanced performance of SSBs present opportunities beyond EV applications including: electric aviation, shipping and even consumer electronics, enabling longer operational life and increased safety.
 
3️⃣Environmental Sustainability:
By minimizing reliance on flammable liquid electrolytes and reducing the demand for scarce minerals, SSBs contribute to lowering the environmental footprint of battery production and disposal, supporting circular economy principles.
 
The global push for solid-state battery innovation reflects a broader truth: clean energy transitions are no longer national ambitions, they are shared imperatives. Strategic investments from India, research partnerships between Brazil & Singapore, and cross-sector collaboration signal a growing recognition that technology must serve inclusive, sustainable development.
 
Solid-state batteries hold the promise not just of better performance, but of decarbonizing mobility, strengthening energy resilience, and accelerating progress toward SDG7. Is the clean energy revolution driving the Global South into a debt crisis?

With the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development Forum underway in Seville, we face a defining global challenge: an annual $4 trillion financing gap threatens progress on the SDGs and a just energy transition.

But this is also a turning point. While clean technologies are more affordable than ever (with 81% of new renewable energy additions more cost-competitive than fossil fuels) less than 15% of clean energy investment reached the Global South in 2023. At the same time, public debt is rising rapidly, threatening to derail both climate and development ambitions. This isn’t just a funding gap; it’s a systemic failure. Yet these signs point to a system on the brink of transformation.

The clean energy revolution is no longer optional; it’s essential. To ensure a fair and inclusive transition, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Reform fossil fuel subsidies: Globally, these reached $1.3 trillion in 2023. Redirecting even a portion of this toward clean energy, health and education could unlock massive development gains - especially where subsidies are untargeted and disproportionately benefit the wealthy.

2️⃣ Redesign public finance frameworks: Mobilizing private capital through blended finance, national development banks, and climate bonds can scale up investments while protecting fiscal space. These tools are key to de-risking investments and scaling renewables in places where markets alone won’t go.

3️⃣ Rebuild global cooperation: This goes beyond aid. We need debt-for-climate swaps, donor-backed guarantees and equitable financing frameworks tailored to the needs of the Global South. Efforts like Egypt’s €54M debt swap with Germany already show what’s possible.

At this FfD Forum, we face a choice: continue financing delay, or fund a just, resilient and sustainable future. The energy transition can either deepen inequality or drive inclusive development. The difference lies in how we choose to finance it.

What if the clean energy transition wasn’t just about cutting emissions - but about redesigning global finance to serve both climate and development?

As the world accelerates efforts to decarbonize, one critical challenge remains under-addressed: the growing tension between debt and decarbonization. Today, many countries in the Global South face a stark paradox - they can’t afford the transition, yet can’t afford to delay it.

With a global financing gap  +$4 trillion annually, the stakes are immense. Today, <15% of clean energy investment reaches the Global South. In Africa alone, the annual need for sustainable energy investment exceeds $200 billion, yet the continent receives just 2% of global clean energy flows.

But what if debt itself could be reimagined; not as a constraint, but as a catalyst for transformation? Here’s what a more equitable financing future could look like:

💡 Reform fossil fuel subsidies - worth $1 trillion in 2023, to free up vital public resources for clean energy, health, and education.

💡 Design smarter public financing frameworks - using tools like blended finance, green bonds, and sovereign wealth funds to mobilize private capital and reduce risk.

💡 Promote debt-for-energy swaps & donor-backed guarantees - aligning financial relief with climate action to unlock new flows of investment in high-need markets.

💡 Strengthen international cooperation - centering equity, supporting local policy design, and accelerating the deployment of clean technologies in underserved regions.

It is time to recognize that debt is not just an economic issue. It is a climate issue, a justice issue, a development issue and ultimately, a survival issue. Without bold, coordinated financial reform, the promise of a global clean energy transition risks remaining out of reach for those who need it most.

Rethinking Fossil Fuel Subsidies: A Lever for Transformative Change in Transport and Society

In Latin America and the Caribbean, fossil fuel subsidies consumed 0.6% - 1.3% of GDP between 2015 and 2021. While traditionally aimed to reduce energy costs for the population, they often fail to reach the most vulnerable and entrench high-emission transport systems.

It’s time to shift the narrative: Fossil fuel subsidy reform is not just a matter of fiscal discipline; it is a strategic development opportunity.

New analysis from UNDP  LAC Latin America and Caribbean  and UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub  outlines a three-step roadmap for governments to redirect subsidies toward low-emission public transport systems that are cleaner, more inclusive, and economically sustainable:

1️⃣ Build strong policy frameworks: Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Ecuador are embedding clean transport into national strategies through transparent fuel pricing and targeted reforms.

2️⃣ Invest in clean mobility: Uruguay’s MOVÉS initiative subsidizes electric buses up to $55K/year. Colombia provides tax incentives for low-emission vehicles. Paraguay links public subsidies to service quality standards.

3️⃣ Mobilize institutions and people: Cross-sector coordination and public engagement are making reforms more equitable, resilient and politically feasible.

Redirecting fossil fuel subsidies is about more than budget reform; it’s a catalyst for long-term social transformation. Sustainable transport systems can improve air quality, reduce inequality and create green jobs across the region.

Offshore wind energy is more than a climate solution; it’s a strategic lever for national development, maritime decarbonization and long-term energy security. By 2030, global offshore wind capacity is projected to reach 212 GW, nearly quadrupling the 73 GW recorded in 2023. Annual additions are anticipated to grow from 9.5 GW in 2023 to over 45 GW by 2030, with China driving half the growth and Europe, the U.S., Japan and Korea emerging as key markets.

Yet, despite this momentum, offshore wind faces high capital costs; long lead times; and permitting barriers - especially in the Global South. These challenges have slowed momentum and shifted investor interest toward faster-moving solar PV projects.
 
Globally, if current commitments are realized, offshore wind could power +1.5 billion homes annually by 2050. But to make this a truly global solution - especially for emerging and climate-vulnerable economies - urgent action is needed across three key areas:

1️⃣ Integrate Offshore Wind into National Energy and Development Plans: Embedding offshore wind in long-term national energy strategies helps align permitting, grid infrastructure, and port development - making projects more investable. In 2023 alone, $33.75 billion was invested in offshore wind globally. With supportive policies, countries can attract a greater share of this capital while linking wind energy to jobs, exports, and green industrialization.


2️⃣ Scale Floating Wind to Unlock Untapped Resources: Traditional offshore wind turbines are fixed to the seabed in shallow waters, excluding many countries with deep coastal zones. Floating wind technology could allow for turbines to be installed further from shore, opening access to major wind resources in regions like Southeast Asia, West Africa and SIDS. As floating technology becomes more affordable, early investment and pilot projects can help bring these regions into the global offshore wind market. 


3️⃣ Use Public-Private Finance to De-risk and Attract Investment: At around $3,461/kW, offshore wind remains nearly three times as expensive as onshore alternatives. Such high upfront costs make it harder for new markets to compete. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can improve project economics and unlock long-term returns. With the right financial tools, offshore wind can scale  in regions where clean energy access is most needed.

Offshore wind isn’t just about clean electricity: it’s about building resilient economies, powering green industries, and creating a just transition.

The Global South holds vast offshore wind potential. With the right policies and partnerships, we can turn this into a catalyst for clean industrialization, energy security, and inclusive growth. #EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #OffshoreWind #MaritimeEnergy

2024 was a milestone year: 17 million EVs were sold globally, making up more than 20% of all new car sales. The clean energy transition is accelerating, and National Innovation Systems (NIS) are ensuring that the Global South is is able to lead at the forefront.

NIS are policy-led frameworks that align government, research, industry and civil society to scale homegrown solutions, build local capacity & drive inclusive growth:

🔹 China: Public investment in brine-based lithium extraction in Qinghai is improving the sustainability and affordability of national battery supply chains. China already refines over 60% of the world’s lithium and leads global battery production.

National Innovation Systems are not just about research; they are tools for sovereign development, job creation and regional resilience. As energy systems become more digital and decentralized, context-specific innovation is essential - from AI solutions suited to tropical climates to technologies that serve Africa’s 3,000+ languages.

Regional interconnection is no longer a technical ambition; it’s a development priority. By integrating electricity markets and infrastructure, Regional Power Pools can reduce energy system costs by up to 23% while enabling near-100% renewable energy penetration.

As energy demand continues to increase - driven by digitalization, electrified transport and industrialization - regional grids offer the scale, flexibility and resilience that national systems cannot deliver alone. But what do these Regional Power Pools look like in practice?

⚡️ Cross-border electricity markets are scaling: In 2022, 9.8 TWh was traded through the Southern African Power Pool, while the West African Power Pool connected 14 of 15 ECOWAS countries under a unified market framework.

⚡️ Transport-energy corridors are being aligned with regional grids: Initiatives like Lobito and LAPSSET are electrifying mineral freight routes to anchor long-term renewable demand and reduce fossil fuel reliance.

⚡️ Structured energy trade between regions are advancing: The CASA-1000 project will enable the transfer of 1,300 MW of clean electricity from Central to South Asia, with commissioning expected in 2025.

⚡️ Collaborative green finance is underpinning integration: A partnership between the AfDB and AIIB is promoting co-financing, co-guarantees, and joint participation to accelerate green infrastructure development across Africa.

Regional integration is not just about energy: it’s about sovereignty, competitiveness and long-term resilience in a climate-constrained world. Explore how Regional Power Pools are shaping this future in the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/ecsVJf4T

While 92% of the world now has electricity, over 666 million people—mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa—still live without it. More than 2.1 billion continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels.

Meanwhile, clean energy investment surpassed $2.2 trillion in 2024, overtaking fossil fuels for the first time. Yet, only 15%—excluding China—reached the Global South. The moment is now to redirect capital where it’s needed most.

Energy is a powerful enabler of transformative change—for people, planet, and prosperity—and the Global South is increasingly at the forefront of this energy revolution.

At the HLPF, it was an honor to represent the UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub at The Future of Energy – Comprehensive Sustainable Energy Solutions for the Global South, organized by Sustainable Development Solutions Network in collaboration with the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition and GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization) . I had the pleasure of discussing how we can accelerate a just energy transition with Prof. Vijay Modi , Elizabeth Nelson , Mr. MEI Feng, Prof. Peter Oviroh , and Mr. Eric F. In 2024, global energy demand grew by 2.2%, exceeding the average growth rate of the past decade—with over 80% of that growth driven by emerging and developing economies.

Progress is accelerating across three key areas:
1️⃣ Integrated energy planning – Kenya’s digital mapping helped expand electricity access from 20% to 75% in just eight years.
2️⃣ Innovative finance and policy de-risking – Mechanisms like feed-in tariffs and concessional capital are cutting financing costs by 25–30%.
3️⃣ South–South cooperation – Now representing over 28% of global trade, it is unlocking faster, more inclusive energy access and investment.

UNDP is proud to work with partners—like Mission 300—to close the energy access gap and accelerate a just, inclusive transition.

These solutions are already transforming lives. The question is no longer if they work, but how fast and how far we can go.

Together, we can turn ambition into fair, equitable, and lasting impact.
